title: Disk, memory and performance
goal: Find what fills the disk, tell space problems from inode problems, read memory and load numbers, and fix the classic "deleted but still open" file.

warmup.q: Write a crontab line that runs `/opt/backup.sh` every day at 02:30.
How do you see the logs of the systemd service `nginx` from the last hour?
Which command finds the 10 biggest numbers, biggest first?

warmup.a: It sends no signal; it only checks that the process exists (exit code 0).

problems.title: What is eating the disk? du and sort -h
problems.situation: The PyTorch training server's disk is 98% full and training has stopped. The user must find, in a few commands, which folders and files are the biggest, before deleting anything.
task: Show the total size of `server` with `du -sh`.
Show the size of each folder directly inside `server`, smallest to biggest (`sort -h`).
Show the biggest folders two levels deep (`--max-depth=2`), only the last 4.
List files bigger than 5 MB with their sizes.
hints: `-s` = summary (one total), `-h` = human sizes (K, M, G).
`du -sh server/* | sort -h` puts the biggest at the bottom.
`find server -type f -size +5M -exec du -h {} + | sort -h`.

explanation.meaning: Disk usage, summary, human units.
One line per folder, sorted by human size (K < M < G).
Show folders down to 2 levels (on a real server: `du -xh --max-depth=1 / | sort -h`).
Stay on one filesystem: do not count `/proc` or other disks.
Find big files and show their size (Day 12).

=== per folder ===

5.1M	server/logs
13M	server/cache
31M	server/model-checkpoints
=== two levels, biggest 4 ===
13M	server/cache
13M	server/cache/pip
31M	server/model-checkpoints

=== files over 5 MB ===

10M	server/model-checkpoints/epoch-3.pt

problems.output_note: The setup created about 47 MB of real files. Run `rm -rf ~/bash-practice/day17` (Reset) when the day is done.
mistakes: Running `du -sh /` as a normal user: hundreds of `Permission denied` lines. Use `sudo du -xh --max-depth=1 / 2>/dev/null | sort -h`.
Using `sort -n` on `du -h` output: `12M` and `4.0K` are sorted wrong. Use `sort -h`.
Deleting files under `/var/lib/docker` by hand. Use `docker system df` and `docker system prune` (Day 26).
problems.interview_say: When a disk is full I run `df -h` to see which filesystem, then `du -xh --max-depth=1 /path | sort -h` again and again to walk down to the biggest folder, and `find -size +1G` for big files.
problems.try_yourself: Run `du -sh ~/.cache 2>/dev/null` and `du -sh ~/bash-practice` on your WSL. Which is bigger?

problems.title: df -h vs df -i: no space, or no inodes?
problems.situation: The app on `/var` fails with `No space left on device`, but `df -h` says `/var` is only 43% full. Every file also needs an inode (a small record with its owner, size and place). If millions of tiny files use all inodes, no new file can be created.
task: Run `df -h /` and `df -i /` on your machine and read the columns.
From `df-snapshot.txt`, print every filesystem at 90% or more.
From `df-inodes-snapshot.txt`, print every filesystem with inode use at 90% or more.
Write down: which mount has a space problem, and which has an inode problem?
hints: `df -h` = space in human units. `df -i` = inodes.
`$5+0` in awk turns `92%` into the number 92.
To find the folder with many files: `find /var -xdev -type f | cut -d/ -f2-3 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head`.
solution: df -i / | tail -n 1 | awk '{print "this machine: / uses", $5, "of its inodes"}'

explanation.meaning: Size, Used, Avail, Use% per filesystem, in human units.
Inodes, IUsed, IFree, IUse% per filesystem.
Make awk read `92%` as the number 92.
A record for one file. A filesystem has a fixed number. Full inodes = `No space left on device` even with free GB.

problems.expected_output:
this machine: / is 24% full
this machine: / uses 2% of its inodes
=== space >= 90% (snapshot) ===
/ 92%
/var/lib/docker 91%
=== inodes >= 90% (snapshot) ===
/var 100%
problems.output_note: The first two lines show the user's own machine, so the numbers are different. The snapshot lines are fixed.
mistakes: Checking only `df -h`. Always check `df -i` too after `No space left on device`.
Deleting one big file to fix an inode problem. The fix is to delete many small files (old sessions, cache files, mail queue).
problems.interview_say: `No space left on device` can mean no free blocks or no free inodes. I check both `df -h` and `df -i`; for inodes I look for folders with millions of small files.
problems.try_yourself: Create 1000 empty files with `mkdir many && touch many/f{1..1000}` and compare `df -i .` before and after.

problems.title: Incident: disk full, but du finds nothing
problems.situation: The backend log grew to many GB. Someone ran `rm app.log` to free space. `df` still shows the disk as full, and `du` shows a tiny folder. The reason: the running app still has the deleted file open, so Linux cannot free the space yet.
task: In `incident`, start a fake app that keeps `app.log` open and writes to it (see the solution, first lines).
Make the log big (20 MB) and check `du -sh .`.
Delete the file with `rm app.log`. Check `du -sh .` again.
Prove the file is still open: look at `/proc/<PID>/fd` and use `lsof`.
Free the space for real: stop (or restart) the app.
hints: A file's space is freed only when no name points to it AND no process has it open.
`ls -l /proc/PID/fd` shows `(deleted)` next to such files. `lsof +L1` lists open files with no name left.
Fix: restart the app, or empty the file through the open handle: `: > /proc/PID/fd/3`.
solution: bash -c 'exec 3>> app.log; while :; do echo "log line" >&3; sleep 0.1; done' &
head -c 20000000 /dev/zero >> app.log        # pretend the log is huge
ls -l /proc/$APP/fd | grep -c '(deleted)'    # ...but the app still has it open
kill -0 $APP 2>/dev/null || echo "app stopped: the kernel can free the space now"

explanation.meaning: The fake app opens the file as file descriptor 3 and keeps it open.
Removes only the name. The data stays while a process has it open.
`du` adds up files it can see by name. `df` asks the filesystem. A deleted-but-open file is counted by df only.
Each open file is a link here. Deleted ones are marked `(deleted)`.
List open files. `lsof +L1` = open files with 0 links (deleted). Often needs sudo for other users' processes.
When the process closes the file, the space is freed.

problems.expected_output:
20M	.
4.0K	.
1
/home/wicky/bash-practice/day17/incident/app.log (deleted)
1
app stopped: the kernel can free the space now
mistakes: Deleting a live log with `rm` to free space. Empty it instead: `: > app.log` (or `truncate -s 0 app.log`). The app keeps writing, and the space is freed.
Rebooting the server for this. Restarting only the app that holds the file is enough.
problems.interview_say: If `df` says full but `du` cannot find the files, a process is probably holding a deleted file open. I find it with `lsof +L1`, then restart that service or truncate the file through `/proc/PID/fd`.
problems.try_yourself: Repeat the steps, but instead of `kill`, run `: > /proc/$APP/fd/3`. Is the app still running? Is the space freed?

problems.title: Memory and load: free, uptime, nproc, vmstat
problems.situation: The API feels slow. The user checks the numbers an interviewer asks about: how much memory is really available, how busy the CPUs are (load average), and whether the server is swapping.
task: Run `free -m`. Then read `free-snapshot.txt`: is that server short of memory?
Print the available memory in MB from `/proc/meminfo`.
Print the load average and the number of CPUs (`uptime`, `nproc`).
Run `vmstat 1 3` and look at the `si`/`so` (swap) and `wa` (I/O wait) columns.
hints: Look at `available`, not `free`. Linux uses free RAM as disk cache (`buff/cache`) and gives it back when needed.
Load average = 3 numbers: last 1, 5 and 15 minutes. Compare them with `nproc`.
Swap used + `si`/`so` not zero = the server is swapping, which is very slow.
solution: echo "=== snapshot from the slow server ==="

explanation.meaning: Memory in MB: total, used, free, shared, buff/cache, available.
How much RAM new programs can get without swapping. The number that matters.
Disk cache. Not wasted: it is released when programs need RAM.
Average number of processes running or waiting. Load 4 on 4 CPUs = full; 8 on 4 CPUs = overloaded.
3 samples, 1 second apart. `r` waiting to run, `si/so` swap in/out, `wa` waiting for disk.

mistakes: Panicking because `free` is small. With 4.5 GB `available`, the server is fine; the cache used the rest.
Comparing load average with 1 on a multi-core server. Always divide by `nproc`.

problems.title: Find the bug: the disk alert script
problems.situation: `disk-alert.sh` reads `df -P` output and should alert for full filesystems. It is tested with the saved snapshot. It prints errors, and it exits with 1 even when nothing is full, so the monitoring always shows red.
task: Run `bash disk-alert.sh 90 < df-snapshot.txt` and `bash disk-alert.sh < df-snapshot.txt`. Read the errors.
Run `bash disk-alert.sh 99 < df-snapshot.txt; echo $?`. Nothing is at 99%, but what is the exit code?
Find 4 bugs: the header line, the `%` sign, the missing default, and the last line.
Fix them and test with 90 and 99 again.
hints: The header has `Capacity` in the pct column: skip lines where pct is not a number.
Remove the `%`: `pct=${pct%\%}`. Default: `LIMIT=${1:-80}`.
`[ 0 -gt 0 ] && exit 1` is false, so the script ends with that false test: exit code 1. Add `exit 0` at the end, or use `if`.
solution: bash disk-alert.sh 99 < df-snapshot.txt; echo "exit code with 99: $?"
# Print ALERT for every filesystem with Use% >= threshold. Exit 1 if there was an alert, else exit 0.
while read -r fs size used avail pct mount; do
bash disk-alert.sh 90 < df-snapshot.txt; echo "exit code with 90: $?"
bash disk-alert.sh 99 < df-snapshot.txt; echo "exit code with 99: $?"

explanation.meaning: Bug 1: `pct` was `Capacity`: `integer expression expected`. Skip non-numbers.
Bug 2: remove the `%` at the end so the test gets a number.
Bug 3: without a threshold, `[ 92 -ge ]` failed.
Bug 4: a script's exit code is the last command's. The false `[ ... ] && exit 1` made it 1.
Reading from stdin makes the script easy to test with saved data. Live use: `df -P | ./disk-alert.sh 90`.

problems.expected_output:
disk-alert.sh: line 7: [: Capacity: integer expression expected
disk-alert.sh: line 7: [: 92%: integer expression expected
disk-alert.sh: line 7: [: 43%: integer expression expected
disk-alert.sh: line 7: [: 91%: integer expression expected
disk-alert.sh: line 7: [: 0%: integer expression expected
disk-alert.sh: line 7: [: Capacity: integer expression expected
disk-alert.sh: line 7: [: 92%: integer expression expected
disk-alert.sh: line 7: [: 43%: integer expression expected
disk-alert.sh: line 7: [: 91%: integer expression expected
disk-alert.sh: line 7: [: 0%: integer expression expected
exit code with 99: 1
--- fixed ---
ALERT / is at 92%
ALERT /var/lib/docker is at 91%
exit code with 90: 1
exit code with 99: 0
mistakes: `cmd && exit 1` as the last line of a script: when `cmd` is false, the script exits 1. Use `if ...; then exit 1; fi`.
Using `df -h` in scripts: units change (G, T) and long device names can wrap lines. Use `df -P` (POSIX format).
problems.interview_say: In monitoring scripts I parse `df -P`, skip the header, strip the percent sign, give thresholds defaults, and make sure the exit code is 0 when everything is fine. I test with saved output on stdin.
problems.try_yourself: Run the fixed script on your real machine: `df -P | bash disk-alert.sh 1`. Every filesystem should alert.

problems.title: lsblk, findmnt and /etc/fstab (read only)
problems.situation: A new EBS data disk was attached to the server and must be mounted at `/data` after every reboot. The user reads the disks with `lsblk`, the mounts with `findmnt`, and the fstab format with a practice copy. The real `/etc/fstab` is NOT changed: a wrong line can stop the server from booting.
task: Run `lsblk` and `findmnt -n -o SOURCE,FSTYPE /` on your machine (read only).
Read `fstab.copy`. Print each line without comments as `mount point -> type (options)`.
Find the line that will not stop the boot if the disk is missing (`nofail`).
hints: fstab columns: device, mount point, type, options, dump, pass.
`grep -v '^#' fstab.copy | awk '{print $2, "->", $3, "(" $4 ")"}'`
On a real server, test a new fstab line with `sudo mount -a` before rebooting.

explanation.meaning: List block devices (disks, partitions) as a tree.
Show what is mounted where, with type and options. `mount` shows the same in a long list.
Use the disk's UUID (from `blkid`), not `/dev/nvme1n1`: device names can change after reboot.
Do not stop the boot if this disk is missing. Important for cloud data disks.
fsck order at boot: 1 for `/`, 2 for others, 0 = skip.

NAME    SIZE TYPE
zram0     0B disk
vda     256G disk
ext4
=== fstab.copy ===
/ -> ext4 (defaults)
/data -> ext4 (defaults,nofail)
none -> swap (sw)
/tmp -> tmpfs (defaults,size=2G)
=== safe if missing ===
/data
problems.output_note: The `lsblk` and `findmnt` lines show the user's own machine. The fstab lines are from the practice copy.
mistakes: Editing the real `/etc/fstab` and rebooting without `sudo mount -a`: a typo can drop the server into emergency mode.
Using `/dev/sdb` in fstab on a cloud VM: after a reboot the name can change and the wrong disk is mounted.
problems.interview_say: To add a disk I find it with `lsblk`, format it, mount it, then add a UUID-based line with `nofail` to `/etc/fstab` and test with `mount -a` before any reboot.
problems.try_yourself: Run `cat /etc/fstab` on WSL (read only). What do you see there?

problems.title: ulimit and "Too many open files"
problems.situation: Under load, the Spring Boot backend logs `java.io.IOException: Too many open files`. Each process has a limit on open files (sockets count too). The user shows the limit and makes the error happen safely in a subshell.
task: Print the open-files limit with `ulimit -n`, and a few other limits with `ulimit -a | head -n 5`.
In a subshell `( ... )`, set `ulimit -n 20` and open files until it fails.
Read the error. Then check the limit outside the subshell: it did not change.
hints: `exec {fd}>/dev/null` opens a new file descriptor and saves its number in `fd`.
The limit in a subshell does not change the main shell.
For services, set `LimitNOFILE=65536` in the systemd unit, or use `/etc/security/limits.conf` for users.
solution: exec {fd}>/dev/null || { echo "could not open more files"; break; }

explanation.meaning: Maximum number of open file descriptors for this shell and its children.
Open one more file descriptor (bash 4.1+).
The process reached its limit. New files and network connections fail.
systemd setting for a service. Docker: `--ulimit nofile=65536:65536`.

problems.expected_output:
open files limit: 20000
real-time non-blocking time  (microseconds, -R) unlimited
core file size              (blocks, -c) 0
data seg size               (kbytes, -d) unlimited
scheduling priority                 (-e) 0
file size                   (blocks, -f) unlimited
bash: redirection error: cannot duplicate fd: Too many open files
bash: /dev/null: Too many open files
could not open more files
limit outside the subshell: 20000
problems.output_note: The limits on the user's machine can be different (WSL often shows 1024 for `ulimit -n`).
mistakes: Raising the limit when the real problem is a leak (the app never closes connections). Check with `ls /proc/PID/fd | wc -l` over time.
Setting `ulimit -n` in `.bashrc` for a service: services do not read `.bashrc`. Use the unit file.

checks.run: ( ulimit -n 20; for i in $(seq 1 30); do exec {fd}>/dev/null || break; done )

problems.interview_say: `Too many open files` means the process hit its file descriptor limit. I check `ulimit -n` and `/proc/PID/fd`, look for leaks, and raise `LimitNOFILE` in the systemd unit if the load is real.
problems.try_yourself: Run `ls /proc/$$/fd | wc -l` to count the open files of your own shell.

interview.q: The disk is full. What do you do first?
interview.a: `df -h` to find which filesystem, `df -i` for inodes, then `du -xh --max-depth=1 /path | sort -h` to walk down to the biggest folders. Delete or compress safely; check for deleted-but-open files with `lsof +L1`.

interview.q: What is the difference between `du` and `df`?
interview.a: `du` adds up the sizes of files it can find by name. `df` shows the free and used space the filesystem reports. They differ when deleted files are still open.
A record for each file with its owner, permissions, size and data location. When all inodes are used, no new files can be created, even with free space.

interview.q: In `free -m`, which column tells you if the server is short of memory?
interview.a: `available`. `free` is small on healthy servers because Linux uses spare RAM as cache.
The average number of processes running or waiting for CPU (or disk) over 1, 5 and 15 minutes. Compare it with the number of CPUs from `nproc`.

recap.meaning: CPU, memory, swap, I/O every second
